decisions.quote:
Both studies’ results partially support Waugh & Norman’s claim, as participants
were more likely to recall a digit that was followed by fewer interfering items. Additionally, we ob-
served an interaction involving presentation rate and interference, as participants performed best
with a low amount of interfering items presented at 1 item per second. However, lists with a higher
number of interfering items (7 and above) had similar correct recall proportion regardless of the
presentation rate.
decisions.reason: The authors state an explicit overall verdict across both Study 1 and Study 2 that their results partially support Waugh and Norman's (1965) claim: recall decreased with more interfering items as in the original, but presentation rate significantly affected recall and interacted with interference at low interference levels, qualifying the original claim that interference alone accounts for short-term memory forgetting.
